research_domain_title: Local Food Capacity, Regional Networks, Value-Added Production, and Food Resilience
note: Broad system architecture for testing multiple models — not a commitment to one food-network structure. Regional Food Network, State Food Exchange, and Community Food Dashboard are design agendas, not operating products. No invented local-sourcing percentages, farmer-income figures, or food-waste statistics. Explicitly rejects an export-only rule for mass-produced staples. Detailed statutes blocked until Phase 2.1 sourced modules.
role_in_philosophy: Food is critical infrastructure and a strategic community asset. Local resilience comes first, regional cooperation second, and national and international trade as complementary strengths — not replacements for strong community food systems. This broadens a single food-network idea into a Community Food Security System that can incorporate and test different models.

rejected_principle.text: Mass production food becomes export only items.
rejected_principle.reason: Large-scale agriculture often produces staple foods efficiently and helps stabilize supply when local harvests fail because of drought, floods, pests, or disease. Making export-only a core principle creates unnecessary isolation and weakens resilience.

central_principle.text: Every community should have the capacity to provide a meaningful share of its essential food needs while remaining connected to broader markets that increase resilience and economic opportunity.

local_first_export_second.text: Communities should have the opportunity to meet local demand before relying exclusively on distant markets, while producers remain free to participate in broader markets.
local_first_export_second.is: An encouragement of strong local food systems.

governing_doctrine.text: Food is a strategic community asset. A prosperous constitutional republic strengthens local food production, supports efficient regional distribution, rewards stewardship of the land, reduces waste, and ensures that every community has reliable access to affordable, nutritious food while remaining connected to wider markets that provide resilience and economic opportunity.

food_as_critical_infrastructure.summary: Food should be viewed as critical infrastructure. Just as a community needs roads, water, electricity, and broadband, it should also have a strategy for fresh food, emergency reserves, local processing, regional distribution, and nutrition. Food security becomes part of public resilience.
food_as_critical_infrastructure.federal_definition_note: USDA ERS defines food security as access by all people at all times to enough food for an active, healthy life — a household/community access concept that Constitutional Capitalism extends into place-based production, processing, and resilience capacity without inventing insecurity rates here.

system_posture.summary: A Community Food Security System gives room to incorporate different models and test what works, rather than committing to one structure from the beginning.
layers: national and international trade as complementary strengths

regional_food_network.summary: Imagine the state divided into regional food districts that cooperate rather than compete for basic food needs.
regional_food_network.illustrative_geography: Arkansas regional food districts are one possible state application — portable doctrine, not a locked statewide map.
regional_food_network.goal: Communities cooperate rather than compete for basic food needs.
regional_food_network.federal_context_note: USDA programs supporting local and regional food markets, value-added products, and food-system infrastructure (including LAMP/food-hub related work) illustrate federal recognition of aggregation, distribution, and market-access tools — not a finished Constitutional Capitalism exchange design.

state_food_exchange.summary: Not government running grocery stores. Government creating logistics infrastructure — a transparent marketplace where farmers list available products and schools, hospitals, senior centers, food banks, restaurants, retailers, cooperatives, and communities can purchase.
aims: improve market access for small producers

keep_value_local.summary: One of the biggest problems is that communities often export raw products and import finished food. Constitutional Capitalism should encourage more local value-added production so more jobs and income remain in rural communities.

fresh_food_networks.summary: Every county could support partnerships that connect farms with schools, hospitals, correctional facilities, universities, nursing homes, and food banks — shortening supply chains and creating dependable markets for local producers.

reduce_food_waste.summary: The philosophy should treat wasted food as wasted human effort. Create systems where surplus food can quickly move to food banks, shelters, schools, community kitchens, and emergency reserves. Technology can match surplus with nearby demand.
reduce_food_waste.federal_context_note: EPA’s Wasted Food Scale prioritizes preventing waste, donation, and upcycling before less preferred disposal pathways — supporting surplus-to-nourishment systems without inventing national waste percentages as doctrine claims.

community_food_reserves.summary: Every region should maintain emergency food capacity — not to replace private markets, but to prepare for natural disasters, transportation disruptions, pandemics, and major crop failures. Resilience is part of prosperity.

regenerative_agriculture_link.summary: Farmers who improve soil health, water quality, biodiversity, and carbon storage could receive payments tied to verified public benefits — aligning environmental stewardship with farm profitability. Connects directly to Resource Sovereignty’s Local Carbon Restoration Exchange.

food_education.summary: Schools and rural academies should teach gardening, soil science, nutrition, food preservation, livestock management, business planning, and food safety. The goal is not that everyone becomes a farmer — it is that every citizen understands where food comes from and how communities remain food secure.

community_food_dashboard.summary: A Community Food Dashboard could track measurable outcomes so communities improve based on evidence rather than assumptions. Indicator slots only until sourced; no invented values.
candidate_indicators: percentage of food sourced locally or regionally
community_food_dashboard.measurement_tools_note: USDA ERS Food Access Research Atlas and Food Environment Atlas are candidate reference tools for later baseline modules — not currently loaded as sourced metric values in this architecture slice.

community_food_security_test.title: Community Food Security Test
community_food_security_test.purpose: Screen food-system policies before acceptance into the framework.

questions.text: Does it increase a community’s capacity to provide a meaningful share of essential food needs?
Does it preserve connection to broader markets for resilience and opportunity?
Does it avoid isolationist export bans that weaken staple-supply stability?
Does it keep more value-added processing and income local where practical?
Does it create dependable markets for local producers without government-run grocery stores?
Does it reduce food waste by moving surplus to people and reserves first?
Does it improve emergency food capacity without replacing private markets?
Does it reward verified land stewardship rather than unverifiable claims?
Does it strengthen food education and civic understanding of food systems?
Can success be measured on a public dashboard without inventing outcomes?

research_status.next: Phase 2.1: deepen ERS/AMS/EPA modules; attach null baseline indicator slots; upgrade diagnosis brief 12; keep Exchange/Dashboard/Network as design agendas; do not invent local-sourcing rates
